answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth (the Count's consignment from Varna via the Demeter to Whitby, consigned to S. F. Billington). All were delivered to the old chapel at Carfax. By 1 October twenty-one had been removed; Bloxam says nine large boxes were carted from Carfax to a house in Piccadilly.

First mentioned on 26 July 1893 in Mina's journal (e0044.1): Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep', and Mrs. Westenra asked Mina to lock their door. The store has no earlier reference; the 'old habit' predates it and is not recorded.

Only one of Lucy's nine entries never mentions Arthur: her diary entry of 12 September 1893 (e0106.1), which speaks of garlic and Van Helsing. The other eight (her letters of 9 and 24 May, 19 Aug, and her diary and memorandum entries of Aug-Sept) all name Arthur.

Four transfusions, in order: (1) 7 Sept, Arthur Holmwood (e0100.5-e0100.8, confirmed by Arthur's own account and Quincey's remark 'Arthur was the first'); (2) 10 Sept, Dr. Seward ('friend John', e0104.2); (3) 13 Sept, Van Helsing, who said 'I shall provide' and rolled up his sleeve while Seward operated (e0107.4, donor inferred from the text); (4) 18 Sept, Quincey Morris, who says 'what I did to-day' (e0116.10).

The garlic came from Haarlem, from Van Helsing's friend Vanderpool's glass-houses, ordered by telegram; a parcel arrived on 11 Sept and a boxful came daily. Van Helsing himself placed the flowers in Lucy's room and made her wreath.

First appears on 5 May 1893 in Jonathan Harker's journal (e0004.1), at Bistritz: he glosses the Slovak and Servian words 'vrolok' and 'vlkoslak' as 'were-wolf or vampire', noting he must ask the Count about the superstitions.

Only one document is in his own hand: his letter of 25 May 1893 to Arthur Holmwood (e0030.1), inviting him to a camp-fire and signed 'QUINCEY P. MORRIS'. Everything else is reported by others, including a line he wrote to Seward, mentioned only second-hand (e0140.1).

experience: The task and grep were the most useful tools. grep gives exact matches with counts, so I could check claims like 'never mentions Arthur' and 'fifty boxes' directly, and list --source with --by-entry showed each narrator's whole output at once, which answered Q3 and Q7 in one call. The snippets in search were truncated at about 200 characters, so the decisive words often fell outside them (for example the donor in the transfusion passages), and I had to read entries in full. The search results also ranked a 'Cutting from The Dailygraph' and unrelated passages high for 'boxes of earth', so semantic ranking was noisy for counting questions. The --limit default of 30 on grep cut off results without saying which were left (it said '7 more not shown'), and I had to raise it. The around command was useful for seeing the speaker's context, though it printed a whole entry where I needed one passage. Two things I wished for: a way to see the matched term in context rather than a fixed-width window, and a way to tell whether a narrator's text was typed, written by hand, or reported by someone else, which mattered for Q7. The date filters were handy for Q6, where I needed the earliest occurrence. The donor in the 13 September transfusion is inferred from the text ('I shall provide') rather than stated outright.
